scores.brief_violations: None hard. All four prices, the exact CTA label (6 times), the FAQ, the footer email, no em dashes or exclamation marks, no external assets. Small liberties: a 'BY HAND' stamp and 'a person will answer' overclaim manual work a little. Mobile puts Standard first in the pricing order.
scores.strengths: The only entry with a truly original concept. It is built like an airmail letter: pale blue paper, perforated edges, a red Knock stamp with a postmark that carries the tagline, and a 'To' address line in the hero that takes target companies inline. That hero field is the best conversion idea in the field. A condensed grotesque headline beside serif body text gives it a voice no other entry has. The sample target-list table under the fold makes the service concrete. The 'Still waiting / return to sender' stamp on the problem list is witty, and the navy How it works band gives the page rhythm. It renders fully in the harness on both views.
scores.weaknesses: The red stamp and 'FOLD HERE' rule sit at the edge of playful, slightly louder than 'calm premium'. The blue-on-blue hero has lower contrast on the small caption text. The Why it works rows are a plain list next to the inventive sections. On mobile the stamp crowds the headline.

scores.brief_violations: No hard violations. Exact CTA label, all prices, FAQ, form and footer are present. The problem card's illustrative reply ('Our team is hiring for exactly this, let me put you in touch') implies an outcome Knock cannot promise yet.
scores.strengths: The most finished execution. The deep green hero with a glowing open door is lovely. The problem section pairs 'Applied, no response' rows with a reply card. The Why it works grid ('60 people', '1:1 every message, one reader', 'Talk first, ask later', 'Proven playbook, borrowed') gets the facts across without inventing stats. Good letter-style example message, tidy pricing with duration and people grids, and a confident dark intake band. The copy is the sharpest in the field.
scores.weaknesses: It lands squarely in the generic template look this brief warns about: dark green, brass and gold, an italic Fraunces serif, cream sections. Everything is executed well, but you have seen it before. The page is a 364 KB client-rendered React bundle, so the static HTML has 33 characters of text: nothing without JS, poor for SEO and resilience. The success state relies on JS role=status only.

scores.brief_violations: None found. Exact CTA label, all prices, FAQ, form and footer email are present. No em dashes, exclamation marks or invented stats.
scores.strengths: The best hero illustration concept: a 10x6 grid of outlined arch doors with one lit and open ('Every company has a door. We find the one that opens'). It is clever, restrained and on-brand. A real process diagram in How it works shows the loop between you and Knock. The Portal vs Door split in the problem section is clear, and the line 'Four steps. You hold the key at every one.' is good.
scores.weaknesses: The cream, condensed serif italic, green and gold palette is the familiar template look. The scroll-reveal is fragile: in the harness's full-page captures the How it works, Why it works and pricing cards render invisible. It works when scrolled, but print, full-page capture and some crawlers miss it. The why-it-works icon cards are generic.

scores.brief_violations: None found. Exact CTA label, all prices, FAQ, form and footer email are present.
scores.strengths: Disciplined and calm. A modern grotesque on a pale sage ground avoids the serif-and-brass cliche. The arch-framed 'Your target list' card (hiring manager, alum two batches ahead, also moved from brand management, director who can introduce) shows the product better than any door drawing. The 60-dot block in Why it works is a nice visual for '60 hand-picked people'. The annotated example message, with numbered underlines explaining why it works, is excellent. Clean pricing and a short form. It renders fully and reads well at 390px.
scores.weaknesses: It is safe to the point of looking like a SaaS template. The typography is competent but not memorable. The problem section is thin, just two short columns with lots of empty space. The hero headline is set small for the space it has. The FAQ and form sections feel like a default kit.

The problem section's grid of closed arches with one lit door ('Most doors stay shut to a cold application') is a good idea. The large 'Why it works' headline, '60 hand-picked people. Not 6,000 messages.' in two tones, has real presence. Good How it works timeline and a dark intake band. It renders fully.

The hero subline mixes grey and bold black mid-sentence, which looks unfinished. Why it works and the pricing cards are fairly plain. The headline weight and the body sans feel mismatched.

scores.brief_violations: None hard. Exact CTA label, all prices, FAQ, form and footer email are present. The hero shows an invented reply from 'Rahul' ('Happy to chat. Free Thursday evening?'), labeled 'Example reply' but still a made-up outcome.

The success message is not in an aria-live region, so screen readers are not told the form went through. There is only a single focus-visible rule. The FAQ heading 'What people ask before they start' hints at a user base that does not exist yet.

judgements.best_ideas_to_graft: 1. Entry-9's 'To:' address line in the hero, which takes target companies inline and carries them into the intake form. It is the strongest conversion device in the field and fits the outreach idea. Its airmail and stamp identity (perforated edge, postmark carrying the tagline) is also the most ownable base for a brand kit. 2. Entry-8's grid of 60 arch doors with one lit open ('Every company has a door. We find the one that opens'), which turns '60 hand-picked people' into a picture without inventing a stat. 3. Entry-1's arch-framed 'Your target list' card and entry-7's 'behind every target company' list (hiring manager owns the role, alumni remember the campus). Both make the service concrete. 4. Entry-1's annotated example message, with numbered underlines explaining why each line works. 5. Entry-2's Why it works grid ('1:1 every message, one reader', 'Talk first, ask later', 'Proven playbook, borrowed'), which gets the facts across without numbers. 6. Entry-9's 'Still waiting / return to sender' stamp and entry-5's 'Pick how many doors to knock on' pricing headline, for door and letter metaphors used with restraint. 7. Entry-4's closing band repeating the north-star promise before the footer. Process note: six entries (4, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12) hide content behind IntersectionObserver reveals that render blank in full-page captures. Any graft should show content by default and only enhance it with motion.

scores.brief_violations: No em dashes, no exclamation marks, exact CTA label, Google Fonts only. Minor: the 'Proven, playbook borrowed' tile makes a claim nobody can check yet. The success state promises a list 'within two working days', an SLA the brief never gave. The problem-section reply card ('Happy to chat. Our team is hiring for exactly this') is labelled illustrative but still suggests outcomes.
scores.strengths: The most premium of the twelve: deep green and brass, a Fraunces italic headline and a glowing open-door illustration. It reads as a private concierge, not software. The problem section shows rows of 'Applied, no response', which hits hard if you have sent 200 applications. The dark example-message section has 'Approved by you / Sent from your LinkedIn' footers that build trust. Pricing hierarchy is clear (Most popular in a brass badge) and the done-for-you card sits beside it. 'We do not guarantee replies. We do guarantee the work' is the most honest line in the competition. FAQ and form are polished, and the form has labels, aria-invalid, a role=status success state and a personalised thank-you.
scores.weaknesses: It is a 364KB React bundle and renders nothing without JS, which is fragile and heavy on a phone. On mobile the hero illustration falls below the fold and the page runs about 10,600px. 'See how it works' is low-contrast text on dark green. The success-state SLA is invented.

judgements.best_ideas_to_graft:
Start from entry-2's look: deep green (#163029-ish) with brass/gold accents on warm cream, a Fraunces serif with italic emphasis and a Figtree-style humanist sans, and the open-door-with-light illustration. Take entry-2's honesty line too ('We do not guarantee replies. We do guarantee the work') and its example card footers ('Approved by you / Sent from your LinkedIn'). Add these:
1) Entry-9's hero inline 'To: your target companies' field next to Get my target list, carried into the full form. It is the best low-friction first step.
2) Entry-1's hero 'Your target list' card (role / reason it matters, labelled as an illustration), or entry-7's 'Behind every target company' card. Either explains the product in 5 seconds.
3) Entry-1's numbered annotations on the Rahul message (specific to him / genuine shared reason / one easy question) and its 60-dot grid for '60 hand-picked people'.
4) Entry-3's grid of shut arches with one golden door for the problem section, or entry-8's 10x6 door grid with one lit. Entry-4's marquee of 'Application #4194 · NO RESPONSE' and entry-2's 'Applied, no response' rows also hit the frustrated applicant hard.
5) Entry-9's mobile pricing order (Standard first) and the CTA repeated in every price card.
6) Entry-6's copy: 'It is not you. It is the channel.', 'Spam is volume without a reason.', 'Still unsure? Write to hello@knock.careers and a person will reply.'
7) Entry-1's code: focus-visible outlines, aria-describedby errors plus aria-invalid, a role=status success state that moves focus, a reduced-motion guard.
Hard rule from this round: never default content to opacity 0 behind IntersectionObserver reveals. Seven of twelve entries (4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12) rendered blank sections because of this. Do not invent SLAs ('within two working days'), outcome replies, or the word 'proven'.
For the brand kit: the field converged on green plus brass on cream, a serif display face with italic accents, and the arch-door motif, which supports that as Knock's identity.

scores.brief_violations: None hard. 'Proven, playbook borrowed' and '1:1' set as display stats next to '60' read like stat tiles and edge toward claims. The 364KB React bundle is allowed by the brief, but it renders the whole page in JS, so with JS off the page is blank.
scores.strengths: Most premium and complete page in the set. Deep green and brass, serif italic headline, a glowing half-open door, all on-brand. Every section in the brief renders in the screenshots. The problem section shows a stack of 'Applied, no response' rows answered by a 'Happy to chat' card. Pricing cards have a clean duration/people grid. The Done-for-you option sits next to the 'Every package includes' list. The FAQ has an intro line with the contact email. The form has placeholders, a personalised success message ('Thank you, {name}. We are on it.') with role=status, a skip link and details/summary FAQ. The scroll respects reduced motion.
scores.weaknesses: Rendering depends entirely on JS, with no static HTML fallback. Heavy bundle for a landing page. Tailwind focus-visible:outline-none appears in places and relies on ring replacements. The stat-style headings in 'Why it works' sit close to invented proof.

scores.brief_violations: None found. No em dashes, no exclamation marks, correct CTA label on all 7 instances, Google Fonts only, no invented stats.
scores.strengths: Confident editorial serif and an illustrated green door with a brass knocker. The problem section has a smart visual: a wall of shut arches with one lit door. Every section renders with no scroll-reveal gating, so the page is robust. Example message has highlighted annotations. Clean pricing plus a Done-for-you card. Form has labels, aria-describedby errors, aria-live success, a skip link and reduced-motion support. Light JS.
scores.weaknesses: The header has no section navigation, only logo and CTA, so How it works, Packages and FAQ can't be reached from the top. The 'Every package includes' list is set as small pills that read like tags. The mobile hero door illustration takes a lot of height. No sticky CTA on mobile.

scores.brief_violations: None hard. The playful 'STILL WAITING / RETURN TO SENDER' stamp and the bright red postage stamp stretch 'calm' a little, but nothing breaks the rules.
scores.strengths: Most original concept: a letter or postcard with 'To:' and an inline target-companies field plus CTA in the hero, the strongest above-the-fold conversion of any entry. A sample target-list table (who, where, shared reason, status) explains the product immediately. On mobile the Standard plan comes first. Best form accessibility: aria-live, aria-invalid, describedby on every field, an inline hero form, a skip link and reduced-motion support.
scores.weaknesses: The powder-blue, navy and red palette is less warm and premium than the green and brass entries and feels more editorial or startup. The 'FOLD HERE' and stamp details are cute but busy. The hero input uses autocomplete=off. The postmark animation adds motion near the headline.

scores.brief_violations: None found.
scores.strengths: Clear, fully visible page. Bold grotesk headline with a brass 'Start conversations.' line. The door has a 'Product, Zepto' plaque and an example reply card. Problem list with NO REPLY tags, then 'Sound familiar?'. Struck-through 'Not 6,000 messages' is a nice touch. Pricing shows days and people as tabular numbers. The success state is personalised with the user's companies and gets focus.
scores.weaknesses: Monospace eyebrow labels ('DOOR 01', 'DRAFT 1, AWAITING YOUR APPROVAL') feel like a developer tool, which undercuts the 'not an AI tool' brief. No aria-live on success or errors. Only 1 aria-describedby, so most error messages are not tied to their fields. The success-heading text swap is not announced. A single reduced-motion block.

scores.brief_violations: None found.
scores.strengths: Every section renders and is easy to scan. The reveal moves elements with transform only, so content is never invisible. That's the most robust scroll motion of any entry. The arch-framed target-list card makes the hero concrete. Footnoted annotations on the example message. Solid form: labels, aria-describedby, aria-live, a skip link and scroll-margin.
scores.weaknesses: Generic SaaS template look: grotesk sans, flat green, icon-in-circle step list and a bento grid. It reads like a software product, not a private concierge. The 60-dot grid is decorative filler. Long mobile scroll with large blank padding. The success heading has outline:none.

scores.brief_violations: None found in source.
scores.strengths: Excellent hero: an 'Your target list, ILLUSTRATIVE' card with shared reasons, '4 of 60 people, researched by hand'. It explains the service at a glance and is on-brand. Content is gated behind a .js class, so it degrades safely without JS. Good form: aria-invalid, describedby, a sample-list next-steps list and reduced motion. Copy is warm and specific.
scores.weaknesses: In both the desktop and mobile full captures, the How it works steps, Why it works grid, example message card and pricing cards are invisible because IntersectionObserver keeps them at opacity 0. The page looks broken and half-empty, and the most important evidence, the packages, can't be seen. Large dead vertical bands.

scores.brief_violations: None found in source.
scores.strengths: Best hero metaphor in the field: a grid of 60 arched doors with one lit ('07 · 03'), and the caption 'Every company has a door. We find the one that opens.' Elegant condensed serif italic. The portal-vs-door comparison card in the problem section is strong. The form renders, with role=status success that gets focus.
scores.weaknesses: .rv{opacity:0} is applied unconditionally, with no .js or no-js gate. If the script fails, the steps, why-it-works, example message and pricing cards stay invisible. In the captures, the steps, a large blank Why panel, the message card and all three price cards are missing. No aria-describedby on form errors. The mobile page is very long with big empty gaps.

scores.brief_violations: None found in source.
scores.strengths: Beautiful hero: a glowing door, a 'Shared reason to talk' card and refined serif italic. Source copy is among the best ('First message, 32 words', 'It is not you. It is the channel.'). The form has a radio package picker plus an edit-details success state. The FAQ uses buttons with aria-expanded and aria-controls. A no-js fallback exists.
scores.weaknesses: Every section below the hero, including the intake form, is blank in both captures because of reveal gating. On mobile the header drops the CTA, and a floating sticky 'Get my target list' button covers the hero illustration card. Collapsed FAQ answers use grid 0fr without visibility:hidden, so screen readers still read them. Global :focus{outline:none}, though focus-visible covers it.

scores.brief_violations: None hard in source. Motion load (cursor-tracking glow cards, door parallax, split-word headings, pulsing rings, scrolling application ticker) conflicts with the 'calm' brief.
scores.strengths: Strong hero: Didone serif, a door with Priya and 'Your reason to talk' cards. A no-js fallback and a reduced-motion override exist. Mobile menu has aria-expanded and Escape handling. Rich ARIA on the form.
scores.weaknesses: Most content is invisible in both full captures: steps, why grid, example message, all pricing and the form. The page is a sequence of empty beige bands. A dim, low-opacity 'Portals are a queue' line fails contrast while it waits for reveal. On mobile, a hamburger replaces the header CTA. Over-animated for a calm, premium service.

scores.brief_violations: None found in source.
scores.strengths: Distinctive condensed serif and an arch card listing 'The hiring manager / The team / Your alumni / Senior people' with roles. The arch-shaped form card is a nice brand echo. The closing 'Knock on the right door.' band is strong.
scores.weaknesses: .reveal{opacity:0} is applied unconditionally with no no-JS gate, so all content depends on JS. In the captures, the problem, how-it-works, why, example and pricing sections are blank, and the form's left-column heading is missing. That's the most fragile implementation among the readable entries. aria-describedby is only used twice. Huge empty vertical space on desktop and mobile.

scores.brief_violations: None found in source.
scores.strengths: Elegant Cormorant headline with a copper italic and a minimalist open-door line drawing with a Priya card. Copy in source is warm and complete, with a 3-step after-submit explainer. A no-js class fallback and focus management exist.
scores.weaknesses: After the hero, both captures show almost nothing: giant black and cream blocks with no text, including the intake form. A visitor or reviewer sees an apparently empty page. Inputs have no placeholders on name and email. The arrow glyph in the CTA is a text character read aloud by screen readers. Contrast of copper on cream is borderline at small sizes.

scores.brief_violations: None hard in source. A '↗' external-link arrow on every 'Get my target list' button wrongly signals leaving the site, and an extra 'Why it works' nav item.
scores.strengths: Refined pill nav and an editorial serif. The five-arches hero card with one open door ('Not every door. The right one.') is on concept. Form errors are written clearly in source.
scores.weaknesses: Worst rendering: nearly the whole page is blank in both captures, including the form, and on mobile even the hero illustration is missing above the fold, leaving a large empty area. Reveal uses filter:blur(8px) plus 48px translate, which isn't compositor-only. input:focus{outline:none} relies on a wrapper ring. Placeholder #8C8276 is low contrast. The ↗ icon on the CTA is misleading.

judgements.best_ideas_to_graft: 1) Entry-9's hero 'To: [your target companies]' field next to the CTA: it starts the intake above the fold and pre-fills the form. 2) Entry-10's 'Your target list, ILLUSTRATIVE' hero card, with a shared reason per person and '4 of 60 people, researched by hand', is the clearest product explanation. Entry-9's sample table (who / where / shared reason / status) also works. 3) Entry-8's 60-door grid with one lit door ('Every company has a door. We find the one that opens.') as the signature visual. 4) Entry-2's palette and door illustration (deep green, brass, light spilling from a half-open arch) and its pricing grid of duration and people contacted. 5) Entry-3's problem visual: a wall of closed arches with one lit. 6) Entry-12's 'First message, 32 words' caption and the radio package picker in the form. 7) Entry-5's struck-through 'Not 6,000 messages' and the success message personalised with the user's companies. 8) Entry-1's transform-only reveal, where content is never set to opacity 0. Use this pattern, or gate on a .js class as entry-10 does, so content can never be hidden; 7 of 12 entries failed full-page capture because of opacity-0 scroll reveals. 9) Entry-9's mobile order with Standard first, and its accessible form (aria-live, aria-describedby on every field, focus moved to the first error).
